idiom_name: goroutine dispatcher + jobs channel + N worker goroutines (close + sync.WaitGroup)
implementation_notes: Go has no separate dispatcher object because the language constructs are the pattern: a jobs channel is the queue, `for msg := range jobs` in N goroutines is the performer pool, and closing the channel is the shutdown signal that terminates every worker's range loop. The dispatcher is itself a goroutine when the selection needs logic (`for { select { case msg := <-in: jobs <- msg } }`), or it disappears entirely when the runtime's scheduler hands each value to exactly one ready receiver. Worker pools sized from runtime.NumCPU() and a sync.WaitGroup for draining are the idiomatic completion contract; the classic hand-written structure is only justified when dispatch must pick a specific worker (per-key affinity, per-worker channels, specialized lanes).
pitfalls: Sending on a closed channel panics, and a worker that panics without recover() takes the whole process down; supervisors and explicit cancellation matter more than in a class-based runtime.
An unbuffered jobs channel makes the sender the dispatcher: it blocks until a worker is free, so throughput is coupled to worker availability and a slow worker stalls the channel.
Goroutines leak when a range loop never sees close() - senders must close, and consumer-side cancellation needs a context or a select with ctx.Done(), not just a closed channel.

The runtime decides which worker receives a buffered value; you cannot steer a specific message to a specific worker through a shared channel - per-key affinity needs per-worker channels and an explicit dispatch decision.
